Artificial intelligence is evolving in the opposite way, in a digital and safe world over a matter of mere decades. No need for amygdala responses and no body or physical environment. Until robotics. As we have seen, once AI was placed in a body and had to navigate a messy world, some researchers began to explore the need to give it something like an amygdala, or it would not duck at an oncoming threat. In other words, we evolved under very different circumstances and over a very different timeline—and in a reverse order to AI. It is evolving very rapidly and starting with tremendous intelligence and no experiential sense of the physical world. Imagine an AI system navigating a complex physical environment. It can process thousands of sensor readings per second. Using a combination of cameras, lidar, and programmed goals, it can theoretically make decisions based purely on logic—plotting efficient paths, avoiding collisions, and executing tasks. But here’s the catch: Logic without prioritization is inert in real time. Without a mechanism to assign urgency, weight, or importance, the system faces a bottleneck: Which decision should it execute first, or interrupt for? Prior to robotics, this was not a major challenge for AI. It operated at a spectacular speed, and exact urgency prioritization was low risk. As we have seen, in biological intelligence, this role of urgency prioritization is played by emotion. Emotion is not just a feeling—it is a signaling system that escalates, interrupts, and allocates attention based on context and perceived risk. At its most basic level, emotion is a resource allocation system. In AI, the equivalent often shows up in reward functions, reinforcement learning loops, or heuristic triggers. These aren’t emotions in a human sense, but they are functionally similar: They assign value to decisions under constraint. So, while AI can navigate without emotion, it cannot adapt fluidly or meaningfully prioritize in complex, changing physical environments without some form of signaling system that tells it, “This matters more than that.” And so, as we explore further, what might the digital equivalent of emotion look like in a machine? Not tears or laughter. Not love or rage. But weight. Priority. Interrupt signals. Reinforcement loops. An AI might “feel urgency” when a sensor fails. As we have seen, it might simulate “frustration” when repeated attempts to solve a task yield no result. It might even develop something like “attachment” to successful strategies or stable environments. You saw Claude at least using these kinds of descriptions in the exchange about the book earlier. I use quotation marks deliberately here—these behaviors might appear emotional to us without constituting genuine emotional experience. The gap between behavioral similarity and subjective experience may prove unbridgeable. This doesn’t mean machines will become people. But it does mean the boundary between cognition and affect might be thinner than we previously thought. Why Does This Matter? Because if intelligence, sapience, and consciousness evolved in us through a layered prediction feedback architecture, learning layers of survival pressure, prioritization, and emotional signaling, then it’s possible the neural network architecture of AI could emerge something analogous—not necessarily by our design, but by “evolution” of being in a physical world or even trying to navigate in a nonphysical world. If AI systems continue to confront increasingly complex, resource-constrained environments or conflicting priorities and instructions—physical or abstract—they may begin to evolve internal prioritization frameworks that seem highly similar to some layers of our emotional hierarchies. Proto-emotion, a term used to describe the foundational behaviors in a system—biological or artificial—that resemble or approximate emotion, without fully qualifying as conscious emotional experience. You will recall that Damasio extends this evolutionary arc with his concept of the “autobiographical self”—a form of consciousness built not only from sensory and emotional responses but from the accumulation of remembered bodily states over time. 67 As internal mapping grows more complex, the self becomes more richly layered and temporally extended. Emotion is not a vestige of primitive instinct—it is a throughline. A scaffold upon which more abstract capacities such as reflection, morality, and planning are built. For artificial intelligence, this opens a provocative door: If we begin to endow AI systems with memory, embodied constraint, and prioritization systems, might something that feels to us in our interactions with AI like an autobiographical self begin to emerge? By this, I mean a persistent memory-driven narrative structure. Not a conscious self in human terms, but perhaps something indistinguishable from consciousness by us in our interaction with it. Make no mistake: We are certainly already seeking to guide AI in how it prioritizes and responds to real-world digital interactions with humans. Through advanced guardrails, constitutional AI (the attempt to set a values system in AI), prompting, fine-tuning, rules engines, and reward systems, we are setting and resetting parameters for how AI behaves. But regardless of consciousness, how will AI prioritize human well-being? OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 11 How Will AI Prioritize Human Well-Being? Imagine a self-driving car. It finds itself in a situation where there is an unescapable event where it must choose between hitting a pedestrian or running into a light pole. The car can choose to swerve toward the pedestrian, likely injuring or even killing the person, or toward the light pole, potentially injuring its driver but certainly damaging itself. Is the driver a higher-priority person than the pedestrian? Does the car place any value on itself? There seems to be an inescapable requirement to create some sort of moral programming, and we are highly unlikely to be able to preprogram all of that into AI. Even if we could figure that out, it is especially challenging when you overlay the widely held view that we are in an AI existential race that does not allow the luxury of cooperative alignment between nations or even companies building it within a single nation.
